title: Numerical method for finding orders
summary: For X + Y -> products at 298 K, three experiments are compared. When [X] doubles with [Y] fixed (experiments 1 and 2), the initial rate doubles, so the order with respect to X is 1. When [Y] doubles with [X] fixed (experiments 1 and 3), the rate stays the same, so the order with respect to Y is 0, giving rate = k[X].

blocks.text: Example. You are given some information about the following reaction at 298 K: X + Y -> products

Experiment | Initial concentration (mol dm^-3) [X], [Y] | Initial rate (x 10^-4 mol dm^-3 s^-1). Rows: 1: 0.02, 0.02, 0.64; 2: 0.04, 0.02, 1.28; 3: 0.02, 0.04, 0.64. Handwritten: x2 arrows between rows 1 and 2 on [X] and on rate, x2 on [Y] between rows 1 and 3, '=' marking rate unchanged.
For the reaction, a) deduce the rate equation for the reaction, and b) calculate the rate constant for the reaction at 298K.
Solution a) From Experiments 1 and 2, under the same initial concentration of Y, initial rate doubles when concentration of X is doubled. Therefore order of reaction with respect to X is 1.
From Experiments 1 and 3, under the same initial concentration of X, initial rate remains the same when concentration of Y is doubled. Therefore order of reaction with respect to Y is 0.

key_concepts: Numerical method: compare two experiments in which only one concentration changes
Rate doubles when [X] doubles: first order in X
Rate unchanged when [Y] doubles: zero order in Y
Rate equation rate = k[X]^a[Y]^b gives rate = k[X]
Orders are found from experimental data, not from the equation

animation.concept: Controlled comparison: pick two experiments that differ in only one concentration, see what the rate does, and read off the order.
animation.why: The page teaches a reasoning method (change one variable, hold the other). Two side-by-side experiment cards with highlighted differences and a rate-bar comparison show this clearly, and it differs from the graph and particle animations on other pages.

steps.caption: Rate doubles when [X] doubles

steps.caption: Experiments 1 and 3: [X] fixed, [Y] doubled

elements: 3 bar meshes for rate (scale 1.28 = full height)
correctness_notes: Exact data: Exp 1: [X]=0.02, [Y]=0.02, rate 0.64; Exp 2: 0.04, 0.02, 1.28; Exp 3: 0.02, 0.04, 0.64 (rate units x 10^-4 mol dm^-3 s^-1; concentrations mol dm^-3)
Always compare experiments where only ONE concentration changes
Order with respect to X is 1; with respect to Y is 0; so rate = k[X] (not k[X][Y])
Orders come from experiments, not from the stoichiometry of X + Y -> products
Page 10 handles the algebraic version of the same data
